## What Is an Employer of Record in Norway


An Employer of Record (EOR) is a third-party organization that becomes the legal employer of your workers in a foreign country. In Norway, that means the EOR signs employment contracts, runs payroll in Norwegian kroner, withholds the correct taxes, and manages statutory benefits on your behalf. Your company retains full control over the day-to-day work: you direct tasks, set goals, and manage performance. The EOR handles the legal and administrative layer sitting underneath that relationship.


Norway has a well-developed labor market with strong worker protections built into the Working Environment Act. Collective agreements, mandatory pension contributions, and generous leave entitlements are standard expectations, not optional extras. Getting any of these wrong carries real compliance risk with[EOR international hiring](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-international-global-hiring-expansion-guide) .


An[EOR removes the need to register](https://www.bolto.com/global-hr) a legal entity in Norway before hiring. Without one, you would generally need to set up a Norwegian subsidiary, a process that takes months and carries ongoing administrative overhead. With an EOR, you can bring a Norwegian hire onto a compliant employment contract in days, not months.


Here is what the EOR typically manages on your behalf in Norway:


- Employment contracts drafted in line with Norwegian labor law and the Working Environment Act
- Monthly payroll processed and filed with the Norwegian Tax Administration
- Mandatory occupational pension (OTP) contributions, which are required by law for most employees
- National insurance contributions paid on behalf of both employer and employee
- Statutory leave entitlements, including vacation pay calculated under the Holiday Act
- Termination procedures, which follow strict notice and documentation requirements under Norwegian law

## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Norway


Norway’s employment framework is one of the most worker-protective in the world, built on a foundation of strong legislation and collective agreements that carry real legal weight. The[Working Environment Act](https://www.arbeidstilsynet.no/en/laws-and-regulations/laws/working-environment-act/) sets the baseline for working hours, termination rights, and employee protections. If you’re hiring there without a full grasp of the rules, the exposure is real.


Here’s how the core requirements break down.


### Working Hours and Leave


Under the Working Environment Act, standard working hours are capped at 9 hours per day and 40 hours per week. Overtime is permitted but tightly controlled, and employees are entitled to a minimum of 25 working days of paid annual leave per year (Ferieloven, 2026). Parental leave in Norway is extensive, with up to 49 weeks at full pay or about 61 weeks at 80% pay split between parents, per[Altinn’s parental benefit guidance](https://info.altinn.no/en/start-and-run-business/working-conditions/print-leave-of-absence-and-holidays/rights-in-connection-with-pregnancy-birth-and-adoption/) .


### Termination and Notice Periods


Norwegian law requires documented grounds for dismissal. Notice periods generally range from 1 to 6 months depending on the employee’s length of service and age. Wrongful termination carries real legal and financial consequences, so documentation and process matter considerably here.


### Collective Agreements


A large share of the Norwegian workforce is covered by collective bargaining agreements (tariffavtaler). These agreements can set terms above the statutory minimums for pay, working hours, and benefits. Employers are generally expected to determine whether a relevant agreement applies to their workforce before setting compensation.


### Social Security and Payroll Contributions


Employers are generally required to contribute to[Norway’s National Insurance Scheme](https://www.nav.no/en/home/rules-and-regulations/membership-of-the-national-insurance-scheme) (Folketrygden). Employer contribution rates vary by geographic zone, ranging roughly from 0% in certain northern regions to 14.1% in the standard zone (Skatteetaten, 2026). Employees also contribute, and payroll is reported through the A-ordningen, Norway’s coordinated payroll reporting system.

## Cost of Hiring in Norway with an EOR vs. a Local Entity


When comparing the cost of hiring in Norway through an EOR versus setting up your own legal entity, the financial picture is usually straightforward: an EOR is faster and cheaper to get started, while a local entity makes more sense at scale.


Here’s how the two approaches break down across the costs that matter most.


### EOR Costs in Norway


The[best EOR companies](https://www.bolto.com/blog/best-eor-companies-global-hiring-guide) typically charge a monthly fee per employee. Industry-wide, fees generally range from $300 to $1,000 per employee per month, depending on the provider and the services included. You avoid the upfront investment of entity registration, and you’re not carrying ongoing costs like local accounting, audit fees, or corporate secretarial services.


### Local Entity Costs in Norway


When comparing a[global employer of record provider](https://www.bolto.com/blog/global-employer-of-record-provider-guide) , note that setting up a Norwegian entity (typically an AS, or Aksjeselskap) requires a minimum share capital of NOK 30,000 (Norwegian Companies Act, 2026). Beyond that, you’re looking at registration fees, legal counsel, a local accountant, annual filings, and ongoing administrative overhead. These costs add up quickly before you’ve hired a single person.


### Side-by-Side Comparison


Cost Factor EOR Local Entity


Setup time Days to weeks Months


Upfront capital requirement None NOK 30,000 minimum (Norwegian Companies Act, 2026)


Monthly admin overhead Included in fee Separate (accounting, filing)


Compliance management Handled by EOR Your responsibility


Best fit Testing the market or small teams Long-term, large-scale presence


The general rule: if you’re hiring fewer than 10 to 15 employees in Norway, an EOR typically costs less in total than maintaining your own entity. Once you’re building a substantial, permanent team, the per-head EOR fee may exceed the fixed cost of running a local entity.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Norway: Which Is Right for You


When you want to hire someone in Norway, you have two realistic paths: set up a local legal entity or work with an Employer of Record (EOR). Each approach has its place, and the right choice depends on your timeline, headcount, and long-term plans in the country.


Setting up a Norwegian entity gives you full direct control. You register directly with the Brønnøysund Register Centre, open a local bank account, and take on payroll, tax reporting, and compliance obligations yourself. For companies planning to hire 20 or more people in Norway over the next few years, this investment often makes sense. The tradeoff is time: entity setup typically takes several months and requires ongoing legal and accounting support.


An EOR lets you hire in Norway without that infrastructure. The EOR becomes the legal employer of record, handling payroll, tax withholding, pension contributions, and labor law compliance on your behalf. Your team member reports to you day-to-day; the legal and administrative layer sits with the EOR.
